Blanche Bruce. Blanche Kelso Bruce was the first African American elected to a full six-year term in the United States Senate, representing Mississippi from 1875 to 1881. A planter, educator, and skilled orator, he navigated the turbulent final years of Reconstruction with pragmatism and dignity.

Bruce was born enslaved in Virginia but educated in the North, where he became a freedmen's school principal before entering politics and acquiring plantation land. In 1874, he was elected by the Mississippi state legislature to the Senate, making him the second Black U.S. Senator overall, but the first to win a full term. Within the Senate chamber, he advocated for civil rights and gave notable speeches defending the rights of freedmen and Indigenous peoples. Later, he served as register of the Treasury under President James Garfield, one of the highest federal offices held by a Black official in the nineteenth century.

Bruce witnessed the collapse of Republican power in Mississippi as Reconstruction ended and white Democrats regained control of state government. After his Senate service ended, he returned to prominence in Republican circles and was appointed minister to Brazil, making him a rare Black diplomatic representative of the era.
